title: Single-Threaded CPU
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning every remaining task at each step versus sorting by enqueue time once and maintaining a min-heap of available tasks by processing time.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given tasks, each [enqueueTime, processingTime], a single-threaded CPU processes them one at a time. At any idle moment, the CPU picks the AVAILABLE task (enqueueTime at or before the current time) with the SHORTEST processing time, breaking ties by the smallest original index. Return the order in which tasks are processed (by original index).

blocks.text: Simulate a single-threaded CPU processing tasks: at any idle moment, it picks whichever already-enqueued task has the shortest processing time (breaking ties by original order), runs it to completion, then repeats.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Single Barista Serving the Quickest Order Among Those Already Placed
blocks.text: Picture a single barista who, whenever free, serves whichever currently placed order takes the least time to make, among orders already placed by that moment, only considering new orders once they have actually arrived.

blocks.caption: Only already-enqueued tasks are eligible; among those, the shortest processing time runs next

blocks.text: Processing in order of shortest available processing time at each idle moment gives the order [0, 2, 3, 1].

Before scanning every remaining task at each idle moment, notice that sorting by enqueue time upfront, and maintaining a min-heap of currently available tasks by processing time, answers "what runs next" directly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A task is only eligible to run once the current time reaches its enqueue time, so sorting tasks by enqueue time lets them be added to an "available" pool in the correct order as time advances.

Observation 2: Among available tasks, the one with the shortest processing time (ties broken by original index) always runs next.

Observation 3: A min-heap of available tasks, ordered by processing time then index, gives that choice directly in O(log n).

Observation 4: If no task is currently available when the CPU goes idle, time must jump forward to the next task's enqueue time, rather than staying stuck.
This leads to sorting tasks by enqueue time, then simulating time forward, adding newly available tasks to a min-heap (ordered by processing time) and always running the heap's top.
At each idle moment, scan every not-yet-run task directly to find the available one with the shortest processing time.

items: Track the current time and which tasks have already run.
At each idle moment, scan every remaining task, keeping only those with enqueue time at or before the current time.
Among those, pick the one with the shortest processing time (breaking ties by index), run it, and advance time.

codes.python:
def get_order(tasks):
    n = len(tasks)
    done = [False] * n
    time = 0
    result = []
    for _ in range(n):
        best = -1
        for i in range(n):                          # scan every remaining task
            if done[i] or tasks[i][0] > time:
                continue
            if best == -1 or tasks[i][1] < tasks[best][1] or (tasks[i][1] == tasks[best][1] and i < best):
                best = i
        if best == -1:
            time = min(tasks[i][0] for i in range(n) if not done[i])
            continue
        done[best] = True
        time += tasks[best][1]
        result.append(best)
    return result

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Every remaining task is scanned directly at each step, to find the best eligible one.
This repeats a full scan for every one of the n tasks processed, redoing much of the same eligibility checking.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), a full scan of remaining tasks at each of n steps.
Space: O(n).
Limitation: re-scanning every remaining task at each step is unnecessary; sorting by enqueue time once and maintaining a heap of currently available tasks avoids repeating that eligibility check.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why re-scanning every task is wasteful: once a task becomes available (its enqueue time has passed), it stays available until it runs; there is no need to re-check tasks that were already determined to be available or not yet enqueued.

What replaces the scan: sort tasks by enqueue time once; as the simulated time advances, add newly available tasks (those whose enqueue time has now passed) into a min-heap ordered by processing time (then index).

What happens when no task is available: jump the simulated time directly to the next task's enqueue time, rather than advancing one unit at a time.

The core idea: sort by enqueue time once, maintain a min-heap of currently available tasks by processing time, and always run the heap's top.

Sort tasks by enqueue time. Simulate time forward: whenever tasks become available (enqueue time at or before the current time), push them onto a min-heap ordered by processing time, then index. If the heap is empty, jump time forward to the next task's enqueue time. Otherwise, pop the heap's top, run it (advancing time by its processing time), and record it in the result.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: sort by enqueue time, min-heap of available tasks by processing time

codes.python:
import heapq

def get_order(tasks):
    n = len(tasks)
    indexed = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: tasks[i][0])   # sort by enqueue time, once
    heap = []
    result = []
    time = 0
    ptr = 0
    while len(result) < n:
        while ptr < n and tasks[indexed[ptr]][0] <= time:
            i = indexed[ptr]
            heapq.heappush(heap, (tasks[i][1], i))              # newly available task
            ptr += 1
        if not heap:
            time = tasks[indexed[ptr]][0]                          # jump to the next enqueue time
            continue
        proc_time, i = heapq.heappop(heap)
        time += proc_time
        result.append(i)
    return result

blocks.text: Sorting by enqueue time once guarantees tasks are added to the available pool in the correct order as simulated time advances; a min-heap ordered by processing time (then index) always exposes exactly the correct next task to run, matching the problem's own rule. Jumping time directly to the next enqueue time when nothing is available avoids wasted simulation steps.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), sorting once plus O(n) heap operations, each O(log n).
Space: O(n) for the heap and result.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "how do you know which tasks are currently available", think: sort by enqueue time once, and add tasks to a heap as simulated time passes their enqueue time.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force runs in O(n squared) time; the optimized sort-plus-heap approach runs in O(n log n) time. Both use O(n) space.

items: Pattern: sort by one dimension (enqueue time), maintain a heap by another (processing time), simulating time forward.
Core Idea: sort tasks by enqueue time; as simulated time advances, add newly available tasks to a min-heap by processing time, and always run the heap's top.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n log n) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: sorting by enqueue time and using a heap for processing time avoids repeatedly re-scanning every remaining task.
Interview Difficulty: a well-known simulation-plus-heap problem, quick once the two-part strategy is recognized.
One line memory trick: sort by enqueue time, heap by processing time, simulate forward.
